title: Reverse a Linked List
statement:
A text editor keeps its undo history as a singly linked list. Each action points to the action that came after it, so the head is the oldest action. The history panel must show the newest action first, so you reverse the list.

A linked list is given as a Python list of its node values, from head to tail; [] is the empty list. Return a list in the same format. In an interview you would get the head node and return a head node; to practise that, build the nodes, move the next pointers, then read the values back.

Write def solution(head) that returns the values of the reversed list, from the new head (the old tail) to the new tail (the old head). Lists can have 100,000 nodes, so avoid recursion.

examples.why: Every pointer turns round, so 5 becomes the head.
The smallest list where a pointer turns: 2 now points at 1.

think.q: What changes when you reverse a linked list, and what stays the same?
think.a: The nodes and their values stay. Only the next pointers change: each one must point at the node that used to come before it. The old tail becomes the new head, and the old head now points at None.

think.q: Reverse 1 → 2 → 3 by hand, one node at a time. What must you remember at each step?
think.a: Node 1: point it at nothing. Node 2: point it at 1. Node 3: point it at 2. Return 3. Before you turn a node's pointer round you must save the node after it, or you lose the rest of the list. So you need three names: prev, cur, and the saved nxt.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: Walk to the tail, unhook it, add it to a new list, and repeat. Each walk is O(n), so the whole thing is O(n^2). Copying the values into an array and rebuilding is O(n) but skips the skill the interviewer wants: turning pointers in place with O(1) extra memory.

In-place pointer reversal. Walk the list once with prev and cur. At each node, save cur.next, point cur.next at prev, then slide both one step forward. The recursive version uses one call per node and would overflow on 100,000 nodes.

1. Build the nodes from the values.
  2. prev = None, cur = head.
  3. While cur is not None: nxt = cur.next, cur.next = prev, prev = cur, cur = nxt.
  4. prev is the new head. Read its values into a list and return it.

The empty list (the loop never runs; return []). One node. Two nodes, the smallest case where a pointer turns. Repeated values (you reverse positions, not values). A list of 100,000 nodes, where a recursive answer runs out of stack.

hints: You need no new nodes. Each node's next should end up pointing at the node that was before it.
Keep two pointers: prev, which starts as None, and cur, which starts at the head. Save cur.next before you overwrite it.
The loop body is four lines: nxt = cur.next, cur.next = prev, prev = cur, cur = nxt. When cur is None, prev is the new head.
explain:
Example 1, 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5. Each row is one pass of the loop:

  • cur = 1: save 2, point 1 at None. Now prev = 1, cur = 2.
  • cur = 2: save 3, point 2 at 1. The reversed part is 2 → 1.
  • cur = 3, then 4, then 5: each points back at the node before it.
  • cur is None. prev = 5, and reading from it gives [5, 4, 3, 2, 1].

At every moment the list is split in two: a reversed part starting at prev and an untouched part starting at cur. Each pass moves one node from the second part to the first, so after n passes everything is reversed. Saving nxt first matters: once cur.next points backwards, it is the only link to the untouched part.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space beyond the nodes

tests.label: one node
tests.why: a single node is its own reverse

tests.label: zeros
tests.why: falsy values must not stop the walk
